headline: Scientists chart new path to restore ocean life through marine rewilding
meta_description: Researchers propose eight principles for marine rewilding to restore ocean ecosystems stressed by overfishing, climate change, and acidification.
summary_short: A new framework moves beyond protection to active recovery of ocean ecosystems, including reintroducing sharks and restoring habitat connectivity.
body:
Ocean ecosystems are gasping under the weight of overfishing, climate change, and acidification. But scientists have moved beyond simply drawing lines around protected areas. In a new perspective paper, researchers including Gavin Stark from the German Centre for Integrative Biodiversity Research propose eight principles for marine rewilding—an active recovery approach that treats oceans like the self-sustaining systems they can become. The shift is fundamental: instead of keeping people out, marine rewilding recognizes that coastal communities are woven into these ecosystems and must be part of the solution.

One concrete success shows the concept working. More than 60 young Indo-Pacific leopard sharks, raised from eggs in a Las Vegas aquarium, have been released into the protected waters of Raja Ampat, Indonesia, to restore balance to coral reef ecosystems. Restoring food webs through reintroducing top predators like sharks is a key principle—one that echoes across all marine environments. Equally vital is strengthening connectivity between fragmented habitats. Just as land animals struggle when forests are broken into isolated patches, ocean wildlife suffers when coral reefs, mangroves, and seagrass meadows become disconnected islands. Protecting migration routes and ecological corridors allows gene flow, supports recolonization, and secures the fisheries and tourism that communities depend on.

The framework also addresses pollution, invasive species management, and adaptive monitoring—tools to help ecosystems not just recover, but become resilient enough to weather future disturbances. For Stark, the goal isn't recreating the past perfectly, but enabling oceans to flourish and self-sustain in the present. "These guidelines are like a blueprint to just start something that maybe will allow this ecosystem to really flourish," he said. Implementation, he emphasized, is the next crucial step.
quick_facts: 60+ young leopard sharks released into Raja Ampat waters, Indonesia
Eight-principle framework guides active ocean ecosystem recovery
Restoring connectivity between coral reefs, mangroves, and seagrass habitats
Reintroduction of top predators like sharks to rebuild food webs
